scenes.title: How skill is actually built
scenes.sub: Deliberate practice · feedback · kind vs wicked · patterns · transfer
scenes.say: Chapter seven. How skill is actually built.
A recall from chapter six. What did repeatedly watching how-to videos do to people's confidence, and to their skill?
scenes.sayA: Confidence went up. Actual skill did not. Only a brief hands-on attempt reduced the illusion.
scenes.a: Confidence up, skill unchanged. A hands-on attempt breaks the illusion.

scenes.text: Deliberate practice: *focused work on specific weaknesses*, with feedback, designed by a skilled teacher.
scenes.note: Necessary, but it explains less than the 10,000-hours story
scenes.say: Deliberate practice, as Anders Ericsson defined it, means focused work on specific weaknesses, with feedback, designed by a skilled teacher. It is necessary. But it explains less than the ten thousand hours story suggests.

scenes.head: How much practice explains, by domain
scenes.say: Across 88 studies, deliberate practice explained about 12 percent of the differences in performance. That varies hugely by domain: 26 percent in games, 21 in music, 18 in sports, 4 in education, and under 1 percent in professions. Among elite athletes, it explained just 1 percent.

scenes.head: The debate

items: Violin study repeated double-blind: the ‘good’ group had practised more than the ‘best’
Practice is one factor of many
Strict deliberate practice: 29%, up to 61% after correction

scenes.say: A double-blind repeat of the famous violinist study, with 39 violinists, did not confirm the original. The good group had actually logged more practice than the best group. Practice is one factor of many. Ericsson's side replies that the critics measured generic practice, and their reanalysis of strict deliberate practice estimates 29 percent, rising to 61 after statistical correction.

scenes.text: Either way, *starting knowledge, working memory and feedback quality* matter alongside hours, and so does how predictable the domain is.
scenes.note: Your levers: feedback loops and mental models
scenes.say: Either way, starting knowledge, working memory, the quality of feedback, and how predictable the domain is all matter alongside volume. Your skills are profession-like. So better feedback loops and better mental models are your levers, more than raw hours.

scenes.head: Feedback helps on average, but…
scenes.say: Across 607 effect sizes, feedback improved performance by about 0.4 on average. But more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse, especially feedback that pulled attention toward the self rather than the task. A 2020 meta-analysis of 435 studies found an average of 0.48, and the more information the feedback contained, the bigger the effect.

scenes.head: Good feedback answers three questions
items: Feedback about you as a person: least effective
scenes.say: Good feedback answers three questions. Where am I going? How am I going? And where to next? Feedback about the person is the least effective kind. For your work, retention graphs, click-through rates, and a viewer saying here's where I lost interest are rich task feedback. Comments praising or attacking you are weak or harmful as learning signals.

scenes.head: Kind vs wicked learning environments
scenes.say: Gut instinct becomes reliable only where the environment is regular and gives fast, clear feedback. Researchers call these kind environments. In wicked ones, feedback is delayed, incomplete or biased, and people gain confidence without gaining skill.

scenes.head: Your skills, from kind to wicked
items: Technical editing: kind. Recreate expert edits shot for shot.
Creative editing: semi-kind. Rebuild sequences, compare 3 editors.
AI prompting: mostly kind. Test 2 or 3 variants on one input.
Scripting and hooks: semi-kind. Daily writing; check 30-second retention.
Ideation and packaging: semi-wicked. High volume; log predictions.
Business: wicked. Hypotheses, cheap tests, a mentor.
scenes.say: No study classifies creator work this way, so this is reasoned inference. Technical editing is kind: recreate expert edits shot for shot, with instant checks. Creative editing is semi-kind: rebuild sequences, and compare three editors. AI prompting is mostly kind: test two or three variants on the same input. Scripting and hooks are semi-kind: write daily, and check 30-second retention. Ideation and packaging are semi-wicked: high volume, and log your predictions. Brand building is wicked, with long-horizon signals. And business is wicked: write hypotheses, run cheap tests, and review them with a mentor.

scenes.head: Experts have pattern libraries
scenes.text: Chess masters recall *real board positions* far better than novices, but ~not random ones~.
scenes.note: Your patterns: hook types, story structures, title formulas, transitions
scenes.say: Experts outperform others not because they have bigger working memories, but because they have libraries of patterns. Chess masters recall real board positions far better than novices, but not random ones. For you, the patterns are hook types, story structures, title formulas and transition styles. Build the library by labelling examples and practising from the labels, not by watching passively.

scenes.bigl: of their decisions experts leave out when explaining their work
scenes.text: So don't ask a mentor *‘what's your advice?’* Ask ~‘walk me through the last time you…’~
scenes.say: Experts also leave out roughly 70 percent of their decisions when they explain how they work. So don't ask a mentor, what's your advice? Ask, walk me through the last time you did this.

scenes.head: Practice transfers mainly to similar tasks
scenes.say: Practice transfers mainly to closely similar tasks. Working memory training transferred to similar tasks with an effect of 0.46, but to different ones at only 0.12. So your practice should look like the real work: real scripts, real edits, real offers.
Your skills are profession-like. If not raw hours, what are your levers?
scenes.sayA: Better feedback loops and better mental models: pattern libraries built by labelling examples and practising from them.
scenes.a: Feedback loops and mental models (pattern libraries)

scenes.say: What should you ask a mentor, instead of what's your advice?
scenes.sayA: Walk me through the last time you did this. Experts leave out about 70 percent of their decisions when they explain.
scenes.a: ‘Walk me through the last time you did this.’
